clue.text: Change the action, if you want to get into an argument.

parts.note: to change something is to alter it

indicators.text: if you want to get into
indicators.note: no word here truly signals the shuffle; the setter lets Change act a second time on action, and this phrase is the only spare wording

parts.note: the letters of action, rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice that switching tactics is the way to pick a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Change gives ALTER, and the setter lets that same word stir ACTION into CATION; there is no separate anagram signal, so 'if you want to get into' is the leftover wording.
explanation.definitionFit: An altercation is a noisy quarrel, so it is a synonym for an argument.

clue.text: Certainly not a 9, being true, but sits awkwardly at last.

indicators.note: at last puts the jumbled sits at the end of the answer

parts.note: to be true to someone is to be loyal

indicators.note: sitting awkwardly means the letters of sits are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of sits, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who is no 9 stays true but squirms uneasily in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkwardly' and 'at last' put the jumbled ISTS at the end. 9 is TORY (9 across); oddly, American colonists loyal to the Crown were themselves called Tories, so 'Certainly not' cuts against history.
explanation.definitionFit: Loyalists are supporters who stay faithful to a ruler or cause, set here against the Tories of 9 across.

clue.text: Time certainly gets rubbed out with it!

parts.note: an era is a period of time
sure, as in 'sure thing', means certainly

explanation.surface: A wry line about time wearing everything away.
explanation.definitionFit: An erasure is the removal of writing by rubbing it out, the act a mark disappears by.

clue.text: Might have ears, but things that hurt your feet speak for themselves!

parts.note: corns are painful hard patches of skin on the feet
to speak is to talk

explanation.surface: A joke that sore feet can complain out loud, as if walls had ears.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid breaks this answer across 4 and 14 down one letter earlier than the wordplay's own break.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn plant's stem carries the ears of maize, so a cornstalk is the thing that bears ears.

clue.text: Workers in the field that steer things.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who till land, farm labourers
second meaning: the bars used to steer boats

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' tempts a reading about cattle in a field; the second sense is the boat's tiller.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who till the soil are tillers, and a tiller is also the lever that turns a rudder.

clue.text: Give something to one on the right when they pass the plate.

parts.note: to offer is to hold something out as a gift
a Tory is a political conservative, on the right

explanation.surface: Church etiquette: hand something to your neighbour on the right when the collection comes round.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on from 6 down into 9 across, the light whose clue reads 'See 6 down'.
explanation.definitionFit: The offertory is the part of a church service when the collection plate goes round the congregation.

clue.text: A very snappy tune, but not much sense in it.

parts.note: hot in jazz slang means lively and fast
an air is a melody

explanation.surface: A catchy song with silly words.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot air is empty, boastful talk, speech with little substance or meaning.

clue.text: Where some hope to find prosperity–just around it.

definitions.text: Where some hope to find prosperity–just around it.

parts.words: Where some hope to find prosperity–just around it.
parts.note: alludes to the Depression-era promise that prosperity is just around the bend in the road

explanation.walkthrough: Herbert Hoover's administration claimed during the Great Depression that prosperity was 'just around the corner'.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying places hoped-for good times at a turn just out of sight, the spot the phrase names.

clue.text: See 6 down
Spring nut? It's a tricky phrase!

parts.note: April is a spring month
a nut is a crazy person, a fool

explanation.surface: A question about a springtime madman, then a comment on a tongue-twister.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on from 10 across into 11 across, the light whose clue reads 'See 10'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'April fool!' is the cry after a prank on 1 April, words that go with a trick.

clue.text: See 10
Without feeling, you get to phone nothing to you and me.

parts.note: to phone someone is to call them
O looks like zero, nothing
you and me together are us

explanation.surface: A heartless person who rings and has nothing to say to us.
explanation.definitionFit: A callous person is unfeeling and hard-hearted, insensitive to others' pain.

clue.text: A manner of carrying this.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one's ... is one's way of standing and behaving
second meaning: ... a load is carrying it

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses share the root of bear, to carry, including carrying oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Bearing is both a person's deportment and the present participle of bear, to carry.

clue.text: See 4
Supposedly pleasing when only man is vile.

definitions.text: Supposedly pleasing when only man is vile.

parts.words: Supposedly pleasing when only man is vile.
parts.note: quotes the hymn line in which every view of a place pleases while only its people are vile

explanation.walkthrough: Reginald Heber's hymn 'From Greenland's Icy Mountains' has 'Though every prospect pleases, and only man is vile'.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is a view or vista, the scenery the hymn says is pleasing.

clue.text: Various way to hang things out in the daylight.

definitions.text: way to hang things out in the daylight
definitions.meaning: second meaning: to ... washing or food is to dry it in sunshine

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the word as two: dry in the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundry means of several kinds, as in 'all and sundry', matching assorted things.

clue.text: Not the old store where the Brits can bet on things.

definitions.text: where the Brits can bet on things

parts.note: not old means new
a market is a place to buy goods, a store

explanation.surface: A new kind of shop where British people place wagers.
explanation.walkthrough: Newmarket is a town in Suffolk, England, famous as the headquarters of British horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: Newmarket's racecourses are where British punters gamble on horse races.

clue.text: Places to get a rubdown with a little writing? They should convulse you!

parts.note: spas are resorts offering massages
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: Spa massages plus some written notes promised to have you in fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Spasms are sudden involuntary muscle contractions, the jerks of a convulsion.

clue.text: Made a face to keep out education, in part.

indicators.note: in part says the answer is only a portion of the run of words keep out education

parts.note: the letters run straight through these three words

explanation.walkthrough: 'in part' signals a hidden answer: it sits inside keeP OUT EDucation, so 'keep out' is not a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To pout is to push the lips out sulkily, a way of pulling a face.

clue.text: One on the workforce has a pole, being concerned with a raise.

explanation.definitionFit: A staffer is a member of an organisation's staff, an employee.

clue.text: A regular go-getter, but you wouldn't want to make a touch with it.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an energetic, enterprising person

definitions.text: you wouldn't want to make a touch with it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a wire carrying electric current, dangerous to touch

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: an electrified wire gives a shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A live wire is a lively, energetic person, and also a wire through which current flows.

clue.text: Green, and mixed up with green outside.

clue.text: Danced, but almost fell over.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: danced a reel, a lively Scottish dance

explanation.walkthrough: Both senses share a picture of whirling feet.

clue.text: Get too big for overcoats, galoshes, and such?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: clothing worn outside other clothes

clue.text: A wild throw, but has some value.

parts.note: the letters of throw, rearranged

explanation.surface: An errant pitch that still counts for something.
explanation.definitionFit: Worth is the value something has, what it would fetch or deserve.

clue.text: Used to announce that person is about to put a message on the channel. You get a wave with it!

the letters of I'd

clue.text: How to hold part of the castle.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to retain it, not let it go

clue.text: Set to be hot or cold.

definitions.text: Set to be hot or cold.

parts.note: describes heating-control devices adjusted to a chosen warmth or chill
